headline: Soup Wars: Local Jingle Decibel Dispute Escalates to Federal Investigation
deck: Suburban rivalries heat up as soup truck complaints turn into a bureaucratic food fight.
article:
Suburban soup rivalries have pulled in federal regulators after repeated complaints about truck jingles. The 3:47 p.m. route log, now filed in triplicate with the Department of Internal Soup Affairs, records 14 violations of the 62-decibel limit. HOA president Tom Spiggle stated, "The Tasty Tuner truck’s jingle disrupts my evenings. My children deserve quiet, not this racket!"

The National Soup Truck Association warned that tighter rules could affect more than 2,300 vending permits. Spokesperson Clara Ladle observed that operators might switch to quieter offerings such as gazpacho to stay within limits.

County mediator Edgar Spooner suggested a shared 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. window for jingle activity. Residents now weigh possible restrictions and some have begun stocking thermoses.
author: Mildred T. Brotherson, Senior Soup Correspondent

oped.title: Decibels for the Downtrodden: Soup Trucks Must Roar Louder
oped.author: Dr. Cornelius Bloviate, Tenured Chair of Auditory Gastronomy and Soup Stock Options
oped.body: Summer heat without ice cream leaves soup trucks as the main source of audible nourishment, yet regulators now probe harmless melodies at the urging of wide-hatted complainers. Those same hats turn mild announcements into personal symphonies of torment. I hold a minority stake in the fleet in question; louder volumes conveniently cover backyard cauldron tests. Equip the trucks with foghorns instead of muzzles so every household receives its minestrone summons. The real monopoly to break is birthday cake’s. Louder soup protects margins and appetites alike.

stories.headline: Decibel Caps Force Soup Truck Chains to Cut Jingle Playtime by Half
stories.deck: BrothMaster shares slide after regulators tie volume limits to sales logs.
stories.article: Federal inspectors have ordered commercial soup vehicles to halve broadcast minutes in suburban zones and log every chime. StewLine Holdings reports a 22 percent revenue drop on affected routes as fewer audible passes reduce customer stops during evening hours.
